approachQuestion.prompt: An input stack has n distinct signed integers, 0<=n<=50,000, in arbitrary order. Only top values may be inspected; the allowed operations are compare exposed values and move one top value between the input and one auxiliary stack. Sort so the smallest is at the input bottom and largest at its top. Return the input stack. Example input bottom-to-top [3,1,2] -> sorted bottom-to-top [1,2,3]. A constant number of local values may be held while moving stack tops. No arrays, recursion or additional containers are allowed.

options.text: Pop each input value x. While the auxiliary top is smaller than x, move that top back to input; then push x onto auxiliary. Finally transfer auxiliary back to input.
options.feedback: The auxiliary stack is maintained in descending bottom-to-top order; transferring it back produces ascending bottom-to-top input.

options.text: Copy values into an array, sort the array, and rebuild the input stack.
options.feedback: The task explicitly forbids accessing values except through stack tops and allows only one auxiliary stack.

options.text: Reverse the input stack by transferring all values to the auxiliary stack and back.
options.feedback: Transferring all values twice restores the original [3,1,2], which is still unsorted; reversal alone also does not establish sorted order.

options.text: On each insertion, move auxiliary tops back to input while they are larger than the held value, then transfer auxiliary back at the end.
options.feedback: This maintains the opposite auxiliary order; the final transfer leaves the smallest value on top rather than at the required bottom.

feedback.reason: The auxiliary stack maintains its order invariant by moving smaller entries aside before inserting x; transferring back yields the requested order.
details: Pop each input value x. While the auxiliary top is smaller than x, move that top back to input; then push x onto auxiliary. Finally transfer auxiliary back to input.

Insertion may temporarily send many smaller auxiliary entries back to input. Those repeated movements distinguish this method from a linear transfer and create the quadratic worst case. The final transfer restores the required stack orientation.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For single-extra-stack-sort, let n be the number of values. Choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. The input stack is working storage and excluded; the one auxiliary stack counts.
constraints: The input stack is mutated and excluded from auxiliary space. No separate output copy is returned.
Each top inspection, comparison, push or pop costs constant time. One auxiliary stack holds at most n fixed-size values and counts as auxiliary space.
Use an iterative implementation with constant scalar locals and no recursion, hashing or hidden copying.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Repeated insertion movements sum to quadratic work with one auxiliary stack.
details: An insertion may move a linear number of auxiliary entries, repeated for n values. The auxiliary stack can hold all n values.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: In reverse-sorted input, successive insertions move an increasing number of entries.
“O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: The auxiliary stack may simultaneously contain n values.
“O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Stack insertion can shift a linear number of values per input value, giving quadratic worst-case work.
